text.p: The British stock market will be vulnerable to turbulence in coming weeks as the general election campaign officially gets underway, strategists said on Monday.
But, they believe, a probable change in government does not point to a sharp turnaround in the fortunes of the booming British stock market.

Analysts say a Labour victory has been priced into London stocks for some time but the market is likely to suffer from a pick-up in volatility as speculation over equity-specific policies intensifies.
The six-week campaign running up to election day on May 1 will be one of the longest in history.

"The length of the campaign drags out uncertainty and creates volatility," said Philip Isherwood, UK equities strategist at Kleinwort Benson. "But the process of discounting has been going on for a long time and the market will try and judge the issues before the actual result."

Three-month implied volatility, a measure of the rate of change of share prices in options on the FTSE 100 share index, is currently around 13 percent. Options traders say volatility had been edging higher over the last couple of weeks.
But during the 1992 election campaign implied volatility on the blue chip index soared to levels of around 30 percent, levels which traders do not expect to experience this time around.

"The election result has already been priced in," said one derivatives specialist. "Volatility will probably edge higher over the coming weeks but the effect will be limited this time by the extent of Labour's lead in the polls."
Labour is currently boasting a lead of around 25 percent in opinion polls having held a substantial lead over the ruling Conservative party for much of the present government's term in office.

"The big thing that could really move the market is if the polls start to show an increasing chance of a hung parliament," said Isherwood, adding that the market's hopes were pinned on a clear outcome.
"The irony is that if the Conservatives continue to do badly in the polls then the market will take confidence from that."
Labour only needs a five percent swing to snatch power and in the Wirral South by-election last month the swing to Labour was 17.2 percent and the turnout one of the highest on record, at 73 percent.
Strategists say the reduced risk to equities is partly due to Labour's more business-friendly front. But many market players will be on guard until specific policy details are spelt out.
"There are equity specific concerns, like the minimum wage, tax credits on dividends and the windfall tax on utilities," said David McBain, UK equity strategist at NatWest.

"As you get closer to the election you're going to see some wobbling and nervousness," agreed Steve Wright, equity strategist at BZW. "People are not quite sure about policy, and specifically what Labour is going to do with regard to the corporate sector."
But with regard to the overall handling of the economy, most strategists remain upbeat.

"The old perception is that Labour tends to be more lax on the fiscal front and that inflation will be a problem," McBain said. "We believe we will see 'new Labour' and they are not going to want to give up the sound economy inherited from (Chancellor of the Exchequer) Mr Clarke."

The market is possibly more vulnerable to swings before rather than after the election if specific policies are laid out on the campaign trail. But the declaration of the result will also remove uncertainty, and it is uncertainty that the market is most at risk from, say strategists.

A recent study by Leeds University of how share prices have reacted under Conservative and Labour governments in post-war Britain show that the largest swings in the market on the day the result was declared coincided with surprise results.
The study found no statistical evidence to suggest that market falls were connected with a specific party.

After the Conservative's surprise win in 1992, the FTSE 30 share index rose 6.2 percent compared with an average 2.1 percent swing in share prices after an expected result, suggesting that the market had priced in results of opinion polls prior to the election date.
But with British stocks standing near record levels, nervousness ahead of the result may stop the market reaching for higher levels.

London's leading FTSE 100 share index has set 17 record closing highs so far this year but strategists say it has already been lagging U.S. and European markets largely because the market has been discounting the prospect of a change of government after 18 years of Conservative rule.
"It will quickly become clear that this is not old Labour and it won't be a return to the 1970's," said NatWest's McBain, commenting on the prospect of a market shake-out.
"There will be a point when confidence is restored," he said.
